title: What Happens If the Strait of Hormuz Reopens?
question: What happens to oil, prices and your money if the Strait of Hormuz reopens after eight months?
description: For eight months the Strait of Hormuz, the route for a fifth of the world's oil, has been almost shut. Now Qatar is pushing a deal and oil is falling. Here is how a reopening would actually work, what it could do to prices in Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas, and what it means for your money. Will the strait be open by the new year? Tell us in the comments.

ad_safety.reason: An ongoing war; handled as economics and diplomacy with no violence shown or described.

scenes.narration: For most of the past eight months, the most important stretch of water in the global economy has been almost shut. On one recent day, ship-tracking data counted just two cargo ships crossing.
This week brought more damaged tankers, a shock result in America's midterm elections, and a new push by Qatar to restart peace talks.

visual.text: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote

scenes.narration: Oil traders moved fast. Brent crude fell almost eight percent on Wednesday, dropping below a hundred dollars a barrel for the first time since early October.

visual.label: Brent crude, $ per barrel
visual.note: Last Friday's high, Tuesday's close, Thursday morning

scenes.narration: So here is the question the whole oil market is asking. What happens if the Strait of Hormuz actually reopens?
The strait links the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, squeezed between Iran on one side and Oman on the other.
Before the war, about twenty million barrels of oil a day passed through it. That is roughly a fifth of all the oil the world uses.

visual.label: of the world's oil use passed through here

scenes.narration: Most of it sailed east. China, India, Japan and South Korea together took nearly seven in every ten barrels of crude.
And it is not just oil. About a fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas trade came this way too, almost all of it from Qatar.
If you want one big story like this explained every day, subscribe. Now, how did one strip of water shake the whole world economy?

visual.text: How did one strip of water shake the world?

scenes.narration: The war began on the twenty-eighth of February, when the United States and Israel struck Iran. Within a week, Iran declared the strait closed.
Iran did not need to sink every ship. A few attacks and the threat of mines made the trip too risky, and insurers stopped covering it.
On a normal day, about eighty-five commercial ships cross. On the twenty-fifth of October, ship-tracking data counted just two.
Here is the key thing about oil: it has one global price. When supply vanishes anywhere, buyers everywhere bid against each other for what is left.
That is why Brent, the world's benchmark crude, hit a hundred and twenty-six dollars a barrel at the end of April, up from about seventy-two before the war.

visual.label: Brent's peak on 30 April, from about $72 before the war

scenes.narration: Governments released four hundred million barrels from emergency stockpiles. It sounds huge, but it is only about four days of the world's demand.
Now Qatar is trying to broker a way out. Its draft plan reportedly sets out three days of confidence-building steps that could restart talks within days.
Iran says it will not reopen the strait until three things happen: the American naval blockade of its ports ends, sanctions are eased, and its frozen money is released.
Iran is already picking favourites. This week a senior Iranian lawmaker said ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar may now pass freely.

visual.text: We have currently exempted India, China, Iraq and Qatar from transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz.

scenes.narration: In Washington, the picture is split. Reports say some advisers want a deal, while others want to keep the blockade, and the military is still preparing options.
Now the scenario. None of this has happened yet. Let's say a deal holds and the strait reopens.
Reopening is not a switch. It is a ladder: talks restart, the blockade eases, mines are cleared, insurers return, and only then do the big tankers come back.
Mines are the slow part. By August, American underwater drones had already identified more than a hundred suspected mines in the area.
Then there is the traffic jam. In May, Saudi Aramco said more than six hundred ships were stuck inside the Gulf, with another two hundred and forty waiting outside.
We have had a preview. In June, when tankers were moving again, Brent sank to about seventy-four dollars. A lasting reopening could pull prices back toward that level.

visual.label: Brent crude, $ per barrel
visual.note: If June repeats itself: an illustration, not a forecast

scenes.narration: First ring: the Gulf itself. Qatar's gas has no other way out, so its exports could restart, and Gulf oil producers could sell at full speed again.
Second ring: Asia. Japan gets about seventy percent of its Middle Eastern oil through this strait, so refiners in Japan, India and China would feel the relief first.
Third ring: everyone else. Oil is still about twenty dollars above its pre-war price, and that gap is built into fuel, flights and shipping costs worldwide.
Cheaper diesel makes trucking and farming cheaper, and fertiliser supplies, which were also disrupted, could recover, easing pressure on food prices.
But there is another branch. Two sources told Reuters they still expect renewed American strikes, and in late April, after talks broke down, oil shot above a hundred and twenty dollars.
So the market swings between two memories: June's seventy-four dollars and April's hundred and twenty-six. Every headline nudges it one way or the other.
So what does all this mean for your money, wherever you live?
Fuel prices usually take a while to follow crude, so do not expect cheaper petrol the day a deal is signed. And if talks fail, prices can rise faster than they fall.
Oil also feeds inflation, and inflation shapes interest rates. Cheaper oil gives central banks more room to cut rates. Another spike could keep borrowing expensive for longer.
A few calm moves work in either branch: keep a few months of essential costs saved, avoid big money decisions on one headline, and budget for fuel and food to swing twenty percent either way.

items.text: No big moves on one headline

scenes.narration: None of this is a prediction, and none of it is financial advice. It is a map of the possibilities, so the next headline does not catch you off guard.
Eight months ago, one narrow strait went quiet, and people far from the Gulf felt it at the pump and at the checkout.
Whether it reopens now depends on talks that have not even restarted, and on steps like mine clearing that take time.
So what do you think? Will the strait be open by the new year, or will the talks fall apart again? Tell me in the comments.
